overview.title: 📖 Overview: Set-Aside Objects and What Frees Them
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 50a–50b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא יִחֲדָן לְהַטְמָנָה, אֲבָל יִחֲדָן לְהַטְמָנָה — מְטַלְטְלִין אוֹתָן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the theme of muktzeh — objects set aside from Shabbat use — and asks what act, thought, or prior use is enough to free such an object for Shabbat handling. Rava rules that wool fleece designated for insulating food may be moved, but Ravina limits this to fleece not taken from a merchant's shelf. Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi disagree about cut palm branches: must one tie them, merely intend to use them, or simply sit on them once before Shabbat? The same question resurfaces with a basket of earth, with cleaning agents like sand and natron, and finally with a pot buried in a basket of wool fleece.

slides.title: 🐑 Wool Fleece: Designated for Insulation or Still Set Aside?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's cover falls off the fleece — does that prove fleece may never be moved?

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: He lifts the cover, and the fleece falls by itself — implying that even fleece used to insulate food may not be moved on Shabbat.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Not so. This applies only where one did not designate the fleece for insulating. If he designated it for insulating food, one may move it — it is no longer set aside.

lines.speaker: Ravina
lines.text: Rava's original statement stands, but the mishna is discussing fleece taken from a merchant's shelves (הֶפְתֵּק) — that fleece is still meant to be returned for sale, so it stays set aside even while insulating food.

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Confirmed: shelf-fleece may not be moved; but if a homeowner prepared fleece for his own use, he may move it.

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: Ownership and intent for personal use — not just present function — determine whether an object is muktzeh.

slides.title: 🌴 Sitting on Cut Palm Branches — Three Opinions
slides.subtitle: Branches cut for firewood, then reconsidered for sitting: what makes them permitted?
rows: Tie the branches together before Shabbat
Agrees with the first tanna: set-aside items need an action to change their status
Merely intend on Shabbat eve to sit on them
Agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: thought alone suffices
Briefly sit on them on Shabbat eve — no tying, no intent needed
Follows the baraita: any use before Shabbat, however brief, permits use on Shabbat

callout.label: Support for Rav Asi:
callout.text: The Gemara finds his view in a Tosefta about wound-dressings used briefly before Shabbat, and in the mishna about straw with a pillow spread on it before Shabbat.

slides.title: 🏺 A Basket of Earth: Is an Action Required?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda permits using earth brought in on Shabbat eve — but what is the rule behind it?

nodes.content: ❓ Rav Yehuda: one may bring in a basket of earth on Shabbat eve and use it all Shabbat, if he designated a corner for it (Mar Zutra)
🤔 The Sages before Rav Pappa: this must follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — the Rabbis require an action, not mere designation!

columns.label: Object CAN be acted on
columns.content: e.g. palm branches — tying is possible, so the Rabbis require it

columns.label: Object CANNOT be acted on
columns.content: earth cannot be 'tied' — so even the Rabbis agree thought alone suffices

nodes.content: ✅ Rav Pappa: even according to the Rabbis, this ruling on earth stands — no contradiction

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: The requirement of an 'action' only applies where an action is physically possible to perform.

slides.title: 🧼 Sand and Natron: Two Baraitot, One Dispute
slides.subtitle: May silver utensils be cleaned with sand and natron on Shabbat?

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda — Prohibits
items: Sand/natron unintentionally smooths and polishes the silver
Two sub-opinions: whether sand actually scrapes at all

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon — Permits
items: Cleaning is the intent; smoothing is a side-effect
Yet even he forbids washing hair with them (may cause hair to fall out)

boxes.title: Practical Face-Washing
items: Rava: ground pepper; Rav Sheshet: berada (aloe/myrtle/violet mix) — none cause hair loss

callout.label: Resolved:
callout.text: Two tanna'im both follow Rabbi Yehuda but disagree only about whether sand and natron actually scrape the silver.

slides.title: 🍯 Removing a Pot from a Basket of Fleece
slides.subtitle: The mishna's dispute: may one lift the pot straight up, or must the basket be tilted?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: tilt the basket on its side so the fleece falls away, then take the pot — lifting straight up risks disturbing the set-aside fleece
2️⃣ The Rabbis: one may simply lift the pot out and later replace it, without tilting
3️⃣ Rav (via Rabbi Abba): everyone agrees that once the cavity in the fleece has actually collapsed, returning the pot is forbidden
4️⃣ Resolution: the real dispute is only whether to be concerned in advance that lifting the pot might collapse the cavity

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Both opinions agree on the underlying halakha; they disagree only on how much preventive concern to apply.

summary.principle: An object set aside from Shabbat use (muktzeh) can be freed for handling by explicit designation, but the amount of preparation required — an action, mere thought, or even brief prior use — depends on the case and the object's nature.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Fleece designated for insulating food may be moved — unless it belongs to a merchant's shelf stock
❓ Palm branches for sitting: tie them (Rav), intend to use them (Shmuel), or briefly sit on them first (Rav Asi)?

columns.content: 🏺 Earth: no action is possible, so thought alone suffices for everyone
🧼 Sand/natron: forbidden per Rabbi Yehuda (unintentional smoothing), permitted per Rabbi Shimon

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the 'action required' rule applies only where an action is physically possible to perform on the object

quiz.q: According to Ravina, why may wool fleece taken from a merchant's shelves (heftek) not be moved even when used to insulate food?
o: It is ritually impure
It is still designated to be returned to the shelf for sale
It belongs to a non-Jew
It was never touched before Shabbat
quiz.e: Ravina explains the mishna is about shelf-fleece, which remains set aside for resale regardless of its temporary use for insulation.

quiz.q: What does Rav Asi require in order to permit sitting on cut palm branches on Shabbat?
o: Tying the branches together
Formally declaring an intention to use them
Briefly sitting on them before Shabbat, even without tying or intending
Nothing at all — they are always permitted
quiz.e: Rav Asi holds that any use of the item before Shabbat, however brief, is enough to permit its use on Shabbat, as shown by the baraita about wound bandages used briefly beforehand.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Pappa say that even the Rabbis (who normally require an action) agree that thinking about using the basket of earth is sufficient?
o: Because earth is not really muktzeh
Because the Rabbis only require an action for objects on which an action is physically possible to perform
Because Rav Yehuda overruled the Rabbis
Because earth was never set aside in the first place
quiz.e: Rav Pappa limits the Rabbis' requirement of an action to cases where a preparatory action can actually be performed; since nothing can be 'done' to loose earth, thought alone suffices.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda, why is cleaning silver utensils with sand and natron prohibited on Shabbat?
o: Because sand is muktzeh
Because it unintentionally smooths and polishes the silver, and Rabbi Yehuda forbids unintentional acts
Because natron is used only for washing hair
Because it is a weekday-only activity
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda holds that an unintentional act (davar she'eino mitkavein) is prohibited, so the incidental smoothing caused by sand/natron makes the cleaning forbidden.

quiz.q: What is the actual point of dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and the Rabbis regarding the pot buried in a basket of fleece?
o: Whether the pot may be eaten from at all
Whether one must be concerned in advance that removing the pot straight up will collapse the fleece's cavity
Whether fleece may ever insulate food
Whether the basket itself is muktzeh
quiz.e: Everyone agrees that once the cavity has actually collapsed, returning the pot is forbidden; the dispute is only whether to be preemptively concerned that lifting the pot will cause the collapse.
